guidance: A starting length from published tubing resistances, not a guarantee: tubing brand, beer temperature, fittings and tower change the real restriction, so cut slightly long and trim until a pint fills in about eight seconds.
method: A draft system is balanced when the resistance between the keg and the faucet cancels the gas pressure pushing the beer, so the beer arrives at the faucet near atmospheric pressure and pours at about 2 fl oz per second, an eight-second pint. The static part is gravity: a faucet above the middle of the keg adds about 0.5 psi per foot of lift, and a faucet below the keg returns the same 0.5 psi per foot, which is why a drop needs a longer line. The dynamic part is the line itself, whose restriction depends on bore and material. The eleven lines in the selector carry the resistance values published in table 4.1 of the Brewers Association Draught Beer Quality Manual, fourth edition: 3/16 in vinyl 3.00 lb/ft, 1/4 in vinyl 0.85, 5/16 in vinyl 0.40, 3/8 in vinyl 0.20, 1/2 in vinyl 0.025, 1/4 in barrier 0.30, 5/16 in barrier 0.10, 3/8 in barrier 0.06, 1/4 in stainless 1.20, 5/16 in stainless 0.30 and 3/8 in stainless 0.12. The line length is pressure minus static resistance minus any tower or fitting resistance you enter, divided by the resistance per foot, with no extra faucet allowance: a 12 psi regulator, a 2 ft lift and 3/16 in vinyl leave 11 psi for the line, which is 3.67 ft. That is the manual's own method, and the page's 11.3 psi example reproduces the 3 ft 9 in direct-draw length in its table 3.3 and the American Homebrewers Association's worked example (12.4 psi less 1 psi of lift over 2 ft, divided by 0.85 lb/ft, about 13 ft). Pressure is limited to 1 to 60 psi, faucet height to -10 to 40 ft above the keg centre, and tower and fitting resistance to 0 to 20 psi; a lift and fittings that consume the whole pressure are refused because no line can balance them. Lengths over 300 ft are refused: a run that long is a long-draw trunk with a choker and blended gas, not a single line. Results are shown in feet and inches to the nearest inch, with feet to two decimals. The resistance table is nominal: the manual itself footnotes it as an example and says to consult the tubing maker, and real restriction moves with brand, temperature and fittings, so the figure is a starting length. The page does not compute carbonation pressure, gas blends, beer temperature, tower resistance or a pour time, and it runs entirely in the browser.
